title: The Second Hand
bodyMd:
**Literary narrative.** This passage is adapted from an original short story. The narrator is a young woman.

My grandfather repaired watches for fifty-one years in a shop the width of a hallway, and when he died the lease had four months left to run. My mother wanted to sell the stock. I said I would sit in the shop until the lease ran out, which sounded, when I said it, like a kindness I was doing for him.

The first week I sold nothing. I learned instead where he had kept things: mainsprings in a cigar box, glass crystals sorted by diameter into the compartments of a tackle tray, and, in the drawer beneath the till, a ledger in which he had written down every watch he had ever been unable to fix. There were eleven of them. Beside each he had noted the owner's name, the fault, and the date he had handed it back.

On the ninth day a woman came in with a watch that had stopped in 1998. She did not want it repaired. She wanted to know whether it *could* be, and she said she would be content either way. I told her the truth, which was that I had no idea, and she left it with me anyway.

It took me three weeks and two ruined balance staffs. When it finally ran, it ran badly, gaining four minutes a day, and I sat with it under the lamp and understood for the first time why the ledger existed. He had not kept it to record his failures. He had kept it so that he would know, if anyone ever came back, exactly where he had stopped.

I telephoned the woman. Then I went to see about the lease.
accessibilityText: A five-paragraph literary narrative told by a young woman whose grandfather repaired watches for fifty-one years in a very narrow shop. When he dies the lease has four months left; her mother wants to sell the stock, and the narrator says she will sit in the shop until the lease runs out, which sounded at the time like a kindness she was doing for him. In the first week she sells nothing and instead learns where he kept his materials, including a ledger in the drawer beneath the till listing the eleven watches he had never been able to fix, each with the owner's name, the fault and the date he handed it back. On the ninth day a woman brings in a watch that stopped in 1998 and asks only whether it could be repaired, saying she would be content either way; the narrator admits she does not know and keeps the watch. After three weeks and two ruined balance staffs the watch runs badly, gaining four minutes a day, and the narrator realises the ledger was not a record of failures but a record of exactly where her grandfather had stopped, kept in case an owner returned. The narrative ends with two short sentences: she telephones the woman, then goes to see about the lease.

provenance.notes: Original literary narrative written for this bank. The narrator, the grandfather, the shop, the ledger and the customer are all invented. Nothing here is drawn from, or modelled on, any ACT-published Reading passage or any published work of fiction.
